t: Colonial rule placed a territory and its people under a distant metropole that ruled them as subjects, through its own officials (direct rule) or through local rulers it controlled (indirect rule).
From Portugal’s capture of Ceuta in 1415 to the eve of the First World War, European empires spread across the Americas, Africa, Asia and the Pacific through conquest, settlement, slavery and trade.
Colonised peoples resisted throughout, from the Haitian Revolution to the liberation wars of the 20th century, and most colonies won independence between 1945 and 1975.
dyk: Britain and France between them traced close to 40 per cent of the total length of the world’s international boundaries.
ev: Portugal captures Ceuta in North Africa, the first overseas conquest of Europe’s colonial age
Spanish conquistadors and their Indigenous allies take Tenochtitlan, capital of the Aztec Empire
The East India Company’s victory at Plassey opens the way to its rule over Bengal
Haiti declares independence after the revolution of the enslaved against French colonial rule
The Berlin Conference opens and sets rules for the European partition of Africa
British India becomes independent as India and Pakistan, amid the violence of partition
The UN General Assembly declares the right of colonial peoples to independence
Angola and Mozambique win independence after Portugal’s Carnation Revolution

f.power: A distant metropolitan state, crown or chartered company, acting through appointed governors, viceroys and officials, and under indirect rule through local rulers it supervised
f.legitimacy: Conquest, treaties made under pressure, papal grants and claims of discovery, justified by a Christian or “civilising” mission and by beliefs in racial superiority
f.chosen: Governors and viceroys were appointed by the metropole; the colonised had little or no say until elected councils, nationalist movements and independence won them representation
f.examples: the Viceroyalty of New Spain (1535–1821), Portuguese Brazil (1500–1822), British India under the Raj (1858–1947), French Algeria (1830–1962), the Dutch East Indies, the Congo Free State (1885–1908)
